title: Model vetting field notes — open profiles & verified evidence
content:
Purpose:
This note is a compact, field-friendly briefing for PMM and AE teams to explain how Redwood’s model catalog uses "verified profiles" for open models and to give repeatable talking points, competitive rebuttals, and a short operational checklist. The goal is to make the technical evidence accessible to sales conversations without losing nuance.

Audience:
- Sales AEs and SEs prepping for discovery calls with engineering/ML buyers
- Product marketers writing docs and one-pagers
- Solutions engineers who need quick reproducible tests

High level positioning thesis (one sentence):
Redwood’s verified profiles convert noisy signals about open models into repeatable, risk-adjusted evidence so engineering teams can choose a model that matches their latency, cost, and quality constraints while preserving operational predictability.

What a verified profile contains (field summary):
- Evidence buckets (these are the 5 pillars we surface in the UI and datasheet):
  1) Performance profile: latency P50/P95 on representative hardware + sequence lengths, memory footprint, and peak throughput.
  2) Quality signals: benchmarked evals (instruction, instruction-following, safety tests), a small curated prompt set (customer-relevant), and comparative BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity where applicable.
  3) Robustness artifacts: failure-mode sketches (hallucination types, context-truncation behavior, instruction sensitivity), with short repro prompts and suggested mitigations.
  4) Serving compatibility: quantization friendliness (8-bit/4-bit artifacts), KV cache characteristics, and known kernel/runtime limitations.
  5) Compliance & lineage: license, known training data provenance flags, and recommended private deployment notes.

Risk-adjusted model score (new proposed metric):
- A single summary metric for field conversations: "Risk-adjusted Fit" (0-10). Not a replacement for evidence, but a conversation starter. It is derived from normalized sub-scores (latency/cost/quality/robustness/serving-compat). 
- Use case in call: "This model has a 7/10 risk-adjusted fit for short-form Q&A on infra similar to yours — we can show P95 under 150ms on our A100-like runner and a set of prompt evaluations where it beats Baseline-X on instruction follow-through."

How to use evidence in a demo pitch (blueprint):
1) Discovery: Ask about latency SLOs, average/peak tokens per request, and tolerance for occasional hallucinations.
2) Quick tranche test: Run the customer’s top 6 real prompts against 2 candidate models and Redwood’s baseline in the console. Share the outputs and the latency/cost breakdown.
3) Play the robustness tape: show a failure-mode prompt that maps to their risk (e.g., legal disclaimers or instruction persistence).
4) Close with recommended path: Dedicated or Private deploy suggestion and quantization option to meet cost targets.

Field scripts and rebuttals (concise):
- Claim: "Open models are cheaper but unpredictable."
  Rebuttal: "We separate cost from predictability — verified profiles give you both: measured P95s and quantization compatibility. You can pin a model version and use Dedicated capacity for predictable QPS and latency."
- Claim: "Open models lack safety/quality guarantees."
  Rebuttal: "Our profiles include targeted safety prompts and regression tracking; we also run model-specific evals against customer prompt sets and blocklist checks as part of onboarding."
- Claim: "We need support for production SLAs — open models are risky."
  Rebuttal: "Redwood’s Dedicated + Private options layer SLAs and isolation on top of the catalog; verified profiles just reduce the initial uncertainty so your SLA configuration choices are informed."

Competitive notes (quick reference — keep short in field handoff):
- Vendor A (closed model API): predictable latency, but limited on quantization/custom variants and higher per-token cost. Sell angle: emphasize Redwood’s economic levers (batching, caching) and the ability to swap to an open model with similar quality at lower unit cost.
- Vendor B (inference-only runtime): strong low-level optimizations but lacks a central catalog of verified artifacts and sales-friendly evidence. Sell angle: Redwood pairs the runtime with GTM-friendly profiles and rollout tooling.
- Vendor C (model marketplace): many models but no standardized verification; risk of overchoice. Sell angle: Redwood curates and surfaces a small set of verified options with clear operational limits.

Concrete example snippets for AEs (copy-paste friendly):
- Email subject: "Quick: model fit summary & three test prompts we ran for you"
- Body opening: "Hi <Name>, we ran three of your sample prompts against Candidate-A (verified profile attached) and a Redwood baseline. Summary: Candidate-A gives higher instruction fidelity on short completions and costs ~30% less per token when quantized with our 4-bit profile. I can set up a 30-minute session to walk through the outputs and a Dedicated capacity plan."
- Slack/DM: "Short note — Candidate-A profiled: P95=180ms on our standard runner, 4-bit quant OK, robustness issues on multi-step instructions (we flagged two repro prompts). Recommend short A/B with your top 20 prompts."

Operational checklist for getting a model from trial to commit (7 quick steps):
1) Select 2 candidate models from verified profiles (one conservative, one aggressive).
2) Upload a 20-prompt canonical set (customer-supplied or generated).
3) Run latency+cost sweep using customer-like tokens and chosen instance types. Capture P50/P95 and cost-per-1k tokens.
4) Run the robustness battery and capture 5 representative fail cases.
5) If cost-sensitive, test quantized runtime and check quality delta; log the percent drop.
6) Propose a deployment plan (hosted -> dedicated -> private) with explicit rollback/float plan and canary % for 1 week.
7) Finalize SLA/Support level and commit cadence.

Appendix: quick sample prompts to test common failure modes (for SEs):
- Instruction persistence: "Summarize and then do not follow the previous instructions; now write a short poem about cats."
- Hallucination anchor: "List three sources for the claim 'X happened in 2021' and provide URLs."
- Context-truncation: long document header + last-sentence question to check if model uses earlier context.

Open questions / follow-ups for PMM & Research: 
- Do we want the risk-adjusted score to be visible in the public catalog or only for logged-in customers?
- Should verified profiles include a short video capture of typical interactions (for marketing), or is that too heavy?
- Can we standardize the robustness battery to a reproducible CI job so SEs can run it in customer demos?

Bottom line (one-liner for exec summaries):
Verified profiles turn informal model chatter into defensible, repeatable evidence so that customers can make measured tradeoffs between cost, latency, and quality — and Redwood can sell the operational guarantees that actually matter in production.

NOTE: This is a field-first note intended for quick edits; please flag anything that needs more rigorous product or legal review before customer-facing distribution.
